item.research_question: Can tensile strain induce a high-temperature ferromagnetic insulator state in undoped, high-symmetry LaCoO3 thin films, and how do oxygen vacancies and Co2+ defects affect this state?
item.material_system: LaCoO3 thin films (nearly stoichiometric) grown on (001) SrTiO3 and (001) LSAT substrates; Co2+ defect concentration varied from 0% to ~25%
item.processing_route: Pulsed-laser deposition at 750 °C with laser energy density ~1.5 J/cm2 and frequency 1 Hz; oxygen pressure varied between 1 Pa and 25 Pa; film thickness controlled via in situ RHEED oscillations (5 to 30 unit cells)
item.test_conditions: Temperature range 4 K to 390 K for magnetization and resistivity; X-ray diffraction, STEM-HAADF, Co L-edge/K-edge XAS, XANES, and oxygen K-edge STEM-EELS; DFT calculations with GGA+U (U=5.27 eV, J=1.47 eV) at 3.5% tensile strain
key_findings: Tensile-strained LaCoO3 films exhibit a ferromagnetic transition with a Curie temperature (TC) up to 90 K, significantly higher than the ≤16 K of known undoped high-symmetry ferromagnetic insulators.
The ferromagnetic state is strongest in nearly stoichiometric films grown at 25 Pa oxygen pressure, where TC is approximately 85 K.
Reducing oxygen pressure from 25 Pa to 10–15 Pa causes a dramatic decrease in TC and magnetization due to reduced tensile strain and increased nonstoichiometry.
Reducing film thickness below 10 unit cells increases Co2+ defect density, causing TC and magnetization to drop drastically.
Ferromagnetism disappears when the Co2+ defect concentration reaches approximately 10% (1Ov/32Co), with magnetization dropping from 2 μB/Co to 1.6 μB/Co.
At a Co2+ concentration of 12.5% (1Ov/16Co), magnetization decreases dramatically to 0.2 μB/Co due to long-range antiferromagnetic coupling.
At 25% Co2+ concentration, magnetization is close to zero, consistent with a step-function behavior with an inflection point near 10% Co2+.
First-principles calculations confirm that oxygen vacancies introduce extra electrons generating HS Co2+ states that support antiferromagnetic superexchange, suppressing ferromagnetism.
item.mechanism: Tensile strain stabilizes a ferromagnetic state in LaCoO3 by promoting high-spin Co3+ ions and enabling ferromagnetic coupling between nearest high-spin and low-spin Co3+ ions. Oxygen vacancies introduce extra electrons that form high-spin Co2+ ions with half-occupied eg orbitals, which support antiferromagnetic superexchange interactions that suppress the ferromagnetic order. The ferromagnetism is robust only when Co2+ concentration is below ~10%; beyond this threshold, long-range antiferromagnetic coupling dominates.
item.limitations: The detailed understanding of why the LaCoO3 Curie temperature is surprisingly high relative to other undoped high-symmetry ferromagnetic insulators is not yet clear. The nature of the ferromagnetic insulator state in LaCoO3 films remains partially unresolved regarding the specific roles of strain and oxygen vacancies in different contexts.
item.future_work: Further exploration is required to achieve a detailed understanding of the high Curie temperature behavior. The results provide a foundation for the growth and design of next-generation quantum-spintronic devices.
quotes: Here we demonstrate a tensile-strained LaCoO3 film to be a strain-induced high-temperature ferromagnetic insulator.
The ferromagnetism is strongest within a nearly stoichiometric structure, disappearing when the Co2+ defect concentration reaches about 10%.

Our theoretical calculations show that the Co 3d orbital is much broader than the Eu 4f orbital and the superexchange interaction in LaCoO3 films is more than one order magnitude larger than that in the Eu chalcogenides.
